title: Parameters
description: Hand values to a method so one method can do the job many ways.

content.value: Telling a Method What to Work With

items: A method with empty brackets always does exactly the same thing.
Put a variable declaration inside the brackets, like `int count`. That is a **parameter**.
The value the caller hands over, like the `3` in `printStars(3)`, is an **argument**.

content.real: A labelled envelope and the letter inside
content.text: The envelope's label, `name`, is the parameter: the slot. The letter you put in, `"Amara"`, is the argument: what goes in the slot.

steps.note: A call with the argument `"Amara"`. Java jumps into `greet`.
The parameter `name` is created and filled with the argument.
Back in `main`. `name` is gone: it only lived inside the method. Now a second call.
The method ends and `name` disappears again.

content.title: Watch the argument travel in
content.outro: The parameter gets a new value on every call.

content.caption: One method, three different results. A method without parameters can only be reused. One with parameters can be adapted.

content.question: In `printStars(7)`, what is `7`?
content.explain: The value you hand over at the call is the argument. `int count` in the header is the parameter that receives it.

items: Each one needs its **own type**, even when two in a row share a type.
Arguments match parameters by **position**, not by name: first to first, second to second.

parts.label: 1st parameter
parts.note: Gets the first argument. Its type is `String`.

parts.label: 2nd parameter
parts.note: Gets the second argument. It needs its own type, `int`.

content.caption: Name parameters for what they mean inside the method, whatever the caller's variables happen to be called.

items.title: Does not compile
items.text: An `int` cannot go into a `String` slot. Java's type checking catches it.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `10` goes into `a` and `3` goes into `b`, so the body works out `10 - 3`.

items: An argument does not have to be typed into your code.
Anything that gives a value of the right type works: a variable, a calculation, or something a `Scanner` just read.
The method never knows where its values came from. That is what makes it reusable.

content.caption: Sample run: type `Mia` and `72`. It prints `Mia | #######` then `A pass.`

A parameter can be any type, even a `Scanner`. Both calls read from the same keyboard: what is passed is the same scanner, not a copy (Module 8 explains why). Create the `Scanner` once, in `main`, and pass it on: a second one on `System.in` causes confusing input bugs. Sample run: type `4` and `9`, it prints `First number doubled is 8` and `Second number doubled is 18`.

content.value: When you pass a number, the method gets a **copy** of it. Changing the copy does nothing to the original.

steps.note: Call `addTen`, handing over the value of `score`.
A new variable `number` starts as a copy: 50.
Inside the method it really is 60.
The method ended, so `number` vanished. `score` never moved.

content.title: Watch the copy change, not the original
content.outro: So `addTen(score);` on its own is almost always a bug. To get a worked-out value back, the method must hand it back: that is the next lesson.

content.value: The copy rule makes methods safe. A method cannot reach out and quietly change your variables, so a bug in one method stays in that method.
content.title: Why this is good

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `n` is a copy of `x`. Setting the copy to `0` leaves `x` at 5.

items.title: Not Java
items.text: Some languages let an argument be optional like this. Java does not compile it.

items.title: Java
items.text: Every call gives a value for every parameter.

items: Java's answer: a second method with the same name and fewer parameters. That is **overloading**, two lessons from here.
Keep parameter lists short. One or two is comfortable, three is fine. Five is a method that wants splitting up.

content.question: How many arguments must every call to this method give?
content.explain: There are two parameters and Java has no default values, so every call gives exactly two arguments, in order.
content.code: static void printBar(String name, int length)

practice.question: Write printRow(char symbol, int count) that prints that symbol that many times on one line, then call it three times with different symbols.
These three blocks are the same code with different numbers. Replace them with one method plus three calls.
Write times(int a, int b) that prints a line like `3 x 4 = 12`, then use a loop in main to call it for the whole 6 times table.
This prints 50 both times. Add a comment explaining why the method cannot change main's variable.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
options: The parameter is the slot in the method, the argument is the value passed in
They are two words for the same thing
A parameter has a type, an argument does not
quiz.explain: `static void printStars(int count)` declares the parameter. `printStars(7)` supplies the argument.

quiz.question: How does Java decide which argument goes into which parameter?
options: By matching the types in any order
quiz.explain: The first argument fills the first parameter. Swap two of different types and it will not compile, which is the good outcome.

quiz.question: A method changes the value of its int parameter. What happens to the caller's variable?
options: Nothing: the method was working on a copy
quiz.explain: The parameter is a separate variable that started with the same value, and it disappears when the method ends.

quiz.question: Can you pass a Scanner to a method?
options: Yes, and both the method and main then read from the same input
No, Scanner can only be used in main
Yes, but each method gets its own fresh copy of the input
quiz.explain: Create one Scanner in `main` and pass it around. A second Scanner on System.in while the first is alive causes hard-to-find input bugs.

quiz.question: How do you write a method whose argument is optional in Java?
options: You cannot: you write a second method with the same name and fewer parameters
Give the parameter a default with `= value`
quiz.explain: Java has no default parameter values. Overloading, coming up shortly, is the replacement.
